title: Python Functions
description: Design functions with explicit inputs, useful return values, predictable scope, and maintainable signatures.

sections.title: Core mental model
sections.learning_objective: Define functions and distinguish parameters from arguments
sections.markdown: A function definition created with `def` binds a callable object to a name. Parameters belong to the definition; arguments are the values supplied by a caller. `return` sends a value to the caller and stops that invocation. Without an explicit return, Python returns `None`, which is different from printing a value for a human.

sections.title: Operations and trade-offs
sections.learning_objective: Use return values, defaults, keywords, *args, and **kwargs
sections.markdown: Positional arguments bind by position and keyword arguments bind by parameter name. Defaults are evaluated once when the function is defined, so use `None` instead of a mutable default such as `[]`. The args kwargs pattern uses `*args` to collect extra positional arguments into a tuple and `**kwargs` to collect extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. Use it when the interface truly needs flexibility, not to hide an unclear API.

sections.title: Worked practice
sections.learning_objective: Trace the concept on concrete data.
sections.markdown: Work from the input and state the invariant before coding. Names assigned inside a function are local unless declared `global` or `nonlocal`. Prefer passing dependencies as arguments and returning results. A pure function depends only on inputs and has no observable side effects, which makes testing easier. Common mistakes are forgetting `return`, mutating caller-owned data unexpectedly, broad signatures, and shadowing a function with another value. For an interview, narrate the observation, the rule you are applying, and the resulting value. That sequence makes reasoning inspectable and exposes hidden assumptions.

sections.title: Common mistakes and fixes
sections.learning_objective: Diagnose failures rather than memorize syntax.
sections.markdown: Names assigned inside a function are local unless declared `global` or `nonlocal`. Prefer passing dependencies as arguments and returning results. A pure function depends only on inputs and has no observable side effects, which makes testing easier. Common mistakes are forgetting `return`, mutating caller-owned data unexpectedly, broad signatures, and shadowing a function with another value. Turn each failure into a focused test. Preserve the original failing input, make the smallest correction, and run the test again. Avoid broad exception handling or a rewrite that hides the root cause.
